question: What is HTML?
answer:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language for creating web pages. It uses tags like

to structure content. HTML defines what is on the page not how it looks.

question: What is CSS?
answer: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls the visual appearance of HTML elements. It uses selectors and properties: p { color: blue; font-size: 16px; }. CSS handles colors fonts layout and animations.

question: What is JavaScript?
answer: JavaScript is a programming language that makes web pages interactive. It runs in the browser and can manipulate HTML (DOM) respond to user events make API requests and update content dynamically.

question: What is the difference between id and class in CSS?
answer: id is unique and used for one element: #header { }. class can be reused on multiple elements: .card { }. In CSS id uses # and class uses dot. id has higher specificity than class.

question: What is the DOM?
answer: The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree representation of an HTML page that JavaScript can manipulate. Use document.getElementById() or document.querySelector() to select and modify elements.

question: What is the box model in CSS?
answer: Every HTML element is a box with content padding border and margin. Content is the actual element. Padding is space inside the border. Border surrounds padding. Margin is space outside the border.

question: What is Flexbox?
answer: Flexbox is a CSS layout system for arranging items in a row or column. Set display: flex on a container then use justify-content for horizontal alignment and align-items for vertical alignment.

question: What is CSS Grid?
answer: CSS Grid is a 2D layout system. Set display: grid on a container then define columns with grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) and rows with grid-template-rows. More powerful than Flexbox for complex layouts.

question: What is responsive design?
answer: Responsive design makes websites look good on all screen sizes. Use CSS media queries: @media (max-width: 768px) { } to apply different styles on mobile. Also use flexible units like % em rem and vw.

question: What is an API?
answer: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a way for programs to communicate. In web development REST APIs send and receive JSON data over HTTP. Use fetch() in JavaScript to call APIs.

question: What is the difference between GET and POST requests?
answer: GET retrieves data from a server and parameters are visible in the URL. POST sends data to a server (like form submissions) with data in the request body. POST is more secure for sensitive data.

question: What is JSON?
answer: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight data format for exchanging data between server and browser. It looks like JavaScript objects: {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}. Use JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify().

question: What is localStorage?
answer: localStorage is a browser API that stores key-value data persistently: localStorage.setItem('key', 'value'). Data persists after the browser closes. Use getItem() to retrieve and removeItem() to delete.

question: What is event bubbling in JavaScript?
answer: Event bubbling means when an event fires on a child element it propagates up to parent elements. Click on a button inside a div and both button and div click handlers fire. Use stopPropagation() to prevent this.

question: What is async/await in JavaScript?
answer: async/await is modern syntax for handling asynchronous code. Mark a function async then await pauses execution until a promise resolves: async function getData() { const res = await fetch(url); return res.json(); }

question: What is a Promise in JavaScript?
answer: A Promise represents a future value. It has states: pending fulfilled or rejected. Use .then() for success and .catch() for errors: fetch(url).then(res => res.json()).catch(err => console.error(err)).

question: What is the difference between let const and var?
answer: var is function-scoped and hoisted (older style avoid it). let is block-scoped and can be reassigned. const is block-scoped and cannot be reassigned. Always prefer const then let over var.

question: What is a callback function in JavaScript?
answer: A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function and called when that function completes: setTimeout(() => console.log('done'), 1000). The arrow function is the callback here.

question: What is semantic HTML?
answer: Semantic HTML uses meaningful tags that describe content: <header> <nav> <main> <article> <footer> instead of just <div>. It improves accessibility SEO and code readability.

question: What is the difference between margin and padding?
answer: Padding is space inside the element between content and border. Margin is space outside the element between the border and other elements. Margin can collapse between elements padding cannot.

question: How does CSS specificity work?
answer: Specificity determines which CSS rule wins when multiple rules target the same element. Inline styles beat ids which beat classes which beat element selectors. !important overrides everything (use sparingly).

question: What is a media query?
answer: Media queries apply CSS based on device properties: @media (max-width: 600px) { body { font-size: 14px; } }. Use them to create responsive layouts that adapt to phone tablet and desktop screens.

question: What is Bootstrap?
answer: Bootstrap is a popular CSS framework that provides ready-made components like buttons navbars cards and a responsive grid system. Add it via CDN and use its class names to style elements quickly.

question: What is the fetch API?
answer: fetch() is a modern JavaScript function for making HTTP requests: fetch('https://api.example.com/data').then(res => res.json()).then(data => console.log(data)). It returns a Promise.

question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
answer: == checks equality with type coercion (1 == '1' is true). === checks strict equality including type (1 === '1' is false). Always use === to avoid unexpected bugs from type coercion.

question: What is a CSS variable?
answer: CSS variables (custom properties) store reusable values: :root { --primary-color: blue; } then use var(--primary-color) anywhere in CSS. They update dynamically and are great for theming.

question: What is z-index in CSS?
answer: z-index controls the stacking order of positioned elements. Higher z-index appears on top. Only works on elements with position set to relative absolute fixed or sticky. Default is auto.

question: What is event delegation?
answer: Event delegation attaches a single event listener to a parent instead of many listeners on children. When a child is clicked the event bubbles up to the parent. Efficient for dynamic lists.

question: What is CORS?
answer: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security feature that blocks requests to a different domain by default. Servers must include Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers to allow cross-origin requests.

question: What is the difference between null and undefined in JavaScript?
answer: undefined means a variable was declared but not assigned a value. null is an intentional absence of value assigned by the programmer. typeof undefined is 'undefined' while typeof null is 'object' (a known quirk).

question: What is the difference between <div> and <span>?
answer: <div> is a block-level element that takes up the full width and starts on a new line. <span> is an inline element that only takes up as much width as its content. Use <div> for sections and <span> for styling parts of text.

question: What are HTML data attributes?
answer: Data attributes store custom data on HTML elements: <div data-user-id='42'>. Access in JavaScript with element.dataset.userId. They are prefixed with data- and are useful for passing information from HTML to JavaScript without using hidden inputs.

question: What is the difference between <script> placed in <head> vs end of <body>?
answer: Scripts in <head> block HTML parsing until they load, slowing page render. Scripts at the end of <body> allow HTML to parse first. Use defer or async attributes on <head> scripts to avoid blocking: <script src='app.js' defer>.

question: What is the HTML <canvas> element?
answer: <canvas> is an HTML element that provides a drawing surface for 2D graphics and animations using JavaScript. Get its context with canvas.getContext('2d') then use methods like fillRect(), drawImage(), and arc() to draw shapes.

question: What is the purpose of the alt attribute on images?
answer: The alt attribute provides alternative text for images: . It is read by screen readers for accessibility, displayed when the image fails to load, and helps search engines understand image content.

question: What are HTML forms and how do they work?
answer: HTML forms collect user input using <form> with child elements like <input> <textarea> and <select>. The action attribute sets where data is sent and method sets GET or POST. Use JavaScript to validate input before submission.

question: What is the difference between <strong> and <b> in HTML?
answer: <strong> indicates text with strong importance — it is semantic and screen readers may emphasize it. <b> is purely visual bold with no semantic meaning. Prefer <strong> for meaningful emphasis and <b> only for stylistic bold.

question: What is an iframe?
answer: An <iframe> embeds another HTML page inside the current page: <iframe src='https://example.com'></iframe>. Used for embedding maps, videos, and third-party widgets. Be careful with security — use the sandbox attribute to restrict iframe capabilities.

question: What are meta tags in HTML?
answer: Meta tags provide metadata about a webpage in the <head>: <meta name='description' content='Page description'>. Key meta tags include charset (encoding), viewport (responsive design), description (SEO), and Open Graph tags for social media sharing.

question: What is the HTML <template> element?
answer: <template> holds HTML that is not rendered on page load but can be cloned and inserted via JavaScript. Useful for reusable UI pieces: const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true). The content is inert until used.

question: What is the difference between position relative, absolute, and fixed?
answer: relative positions an element relative to its normal position without removing it from flow. absolute positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor and removes it from flow. fixed positions it relative to the viewport — it stays put when scrolling.

question: What are CSS pseudo-classes?
answer: Pseudo-classes style elements based on state: a:hover { color: red; } styles links on hover. Common ones include :focus :active :first-child :last-child :nth-child(n) and :not(). They add interactivity without JavaScript.

question: What are CSS pseudo-elements?
answer: Pseudo-elements style specific parts of elements. ::before and ::after insert content before or after an element's content. ::first-letter styles the first letter. ::placeholder styles input placeholder text. They use double colons (::).

question: What is the CSS transition property?
answer: transition animates CSS property changes smoothly: transition: background-color 0.3s ease. Define the property duration timing-function and delay. Combine with :hover or class changes triggered by JavaScript for interactive UI effects.

question: What is the CSS animation property?
answer: CSS animations use @keyframes to define states: @keyframes spin { from { transform: rotate(0deg); } to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }. Apply with: animation: spin 1s linear infinite. More powerful than transitions for complex multi-step animations.

question: What is the difference between em and rem units in CSS?
answer: em is relative to the font size of the parent element — it compounds in nested elements. rem is relative to the root <html> element font size (usually 16px). rem is more predictable for consistent sizing across the page.

question: What is CSS specificity and how is it calculated?
answer: Specificity is a score that determines which CSS rule wins. Inline styles score 1000, IDs score 100, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes score 10, and elements/pseudo-elements score 1. The rule with the highest total score wins.

question: What is the CSS display property?
answer: display controls how an element is rendered. block takes full width and starts on a new line. inline flows with text. inline-block is inline but accepts width and height. flex and grid enable layout systems. none hides the element completely.

question: What is the CSS overflow property?
answer: overflow controls what happens when content is larger than its container. visible shows all content (default). hidden clips it. scroll always shows scrollbars. auto adds scrollbars only when needed. overflow-x and overflow-y control axes separately.

question: What is the CSS calc() function?
answer: calc() performs math mixing different units: width: calc(100% - 80px). Useful for dynamic sizing that cannot be expressed with a single unit. Supports addition subtraction multiplication and division. Works for any CSS property that accepts length values.

question: What is the will-change CSS property?
answer: will-change hints to the browser that an element will be animated, letting it optimize rendering ahead of time: will-change: transform. Use sparingly — applying it to too many elements wastes memory. Only add it when you know an animation is about to happen.

question: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
answer: Hoisting moves variable and function declarations to the top of their scope before code runs. var declarations are hoisted (but not their values). Function declarations are fully hoisted. let and const are hoisted but not initialized — accessing them before declaration causes a ReferenceError.

question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
answer: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function returns: function counter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }. The returned arrow function closes over n. Closures enable data privacy and factory functions.

question: What is the spread operator in JavaScript?
answer: The spread operator (...) expands an iterable into individual elements. Copy arrays: [...arr]. Merge arrays: [...a, ...b]. Pass array as arguments: Math.max(...numbers). Spread also works with objects: { ...obj, newKey: value } to merge or override properties.

question: What is destructuring in JavaScript?
answer: Destructuring extracts values from arrays or objects into variables. Array: const [a, b] = [1, 2]. Object: const { name, age } = person. You can rename: const { name: fullName } = person and provide defaults: const { age = 18 } = person.

question: What is the difference between map, filter, and reduce?
answer: map transforms each array element and returns a new array. filter returns a new array with elements that pass a test. reduce accumulates array elements into a single value. All three are non-mutating and take callback functions.

question: What is event loop in JavaScript?
answer: The event loop lets JavaScript handle async operations despite being single-threaded. It continuously checks the call stack and the task queue. When the stack is empty it pushes queued callbacks (setTimeout, fetch responses) onto the stack to execute.

question: What are arrow functions in JavaScript?
answer: Arrow functions are a shorter function syntax: const add = (a, b) => a + b. They do not have their own this — they inherit it from the surrounding context. They cannot be used as constructors and have no arguments object.

question: What is the difference between forEach and map in JavaScript?
answer: forEach iterates over an array and executes a callback for each element but returns undefined. map also iterates but returns a new array of transformed values. Use map when you need the results and forEach for side effects like logging or DOM updates.

question: What is prototype in JavaScript?
answer: Every JavaScript object has a prototype — an object it inherits methods and properties from. When you access a property the engine walks up the prototype chain until it finds it or reaches null. Array methods like push and map live on Array.prototype.

question: What is the this keyword in JavaScript?
answer: this refers to the current execution context. In a method it refers to the object. In a regular function it refers to the global object (or undefined in strict mode). Arrow functions inherit this from their enclosing scope. Use bind() call() or apply() to set this explicitly.

question: What are template literals in JavaScript?
answer: Template literals use backticks and allow embedded expressions: const msg = `Hello ${name}, you are ${age} years old`. They support multi-line strings without \n and tagged templates for advanced string processing.

question: What is optional chaining in JavaScript?
answer: Optional chaining (?.) safely accesses nested properties without throwing if an intermediate value is null or undefined: user?.address?.city returns undefined instead of crashing. Works with method calls (obj.method?.()) and array access (arr?.[0]).

question: What is the nullish coalescing operator in JavaScript?
answer: The nullish coalescing operator (??) returns the right-hand value only when the left is null or undefined: const name = user.name ?? 'Guest'. Unlike ||, it does not treat 0 or empty string as falsy, making it safer for default values.

question: What is the difference between sessionStorage and localStorage?
answer: Both store key-value pairs in the browser. localStorage persists until explicitly cleared — even after the browser closes. sessionStorage is cleared when the tab or browser is closed. Both are limited to about 5MB and are domain-specific.

question: What are cookies and how are they different from localStorage?
answer: Cookies are small data pieces sent with every HTTP request to the server, used for authentication and sessions. localStorage is client-only and not sent to the server. Cookies have expiry dates and size limits (~4KB). Use cookies for server-needed data and localStorage for client-only data.

question: What is the Fetch API and how does error handling work?
answer: fetch() returns a Promise that resolves with a Response object. Unlike axios, fetch does not reject on HTTP error codes like 404 or 500 — only on network failure. Always check res.ok or res.status: if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.statusText).

question: What is the MutationObserver API?
answer: MutationObserver watches for changes to the DOM: const obs = new MutationObserver(callback); obs.observe(targetNode, { childList: true, subtree: true }). Useful for reacting to DOM changes made by third-party code without polling with setInterval.

question: What is the IntersectionObserver API?
answer: IntersectionObserver detects when an element enters or exits the viewport: new IntersectionObserver(callback).observe(element). Used for lazy loading images, infinite scroll, and triggering animations when elements become visible without scroll event listeners.

question: What is the History API in browsers?
answer: The History API lets you manipulate the browser history without full page reloads. history.pushState(state, title, url) adds a new entry. history.replaceState() updates the current entry. The popstate event fires when the user navigates back or forward. Used in single-page applications.

question: What is a Service Worker?
answer: A Service Worker is a script that runs in the background separate from the web page. It intercepts network requests, enables offline caching, and powers push notifications. It is the foundation of Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) and uses the Cache API to store assets.

question: What is the Web Storage API?
answer: The Web Storage API provides localStorage and sessionStorage for storing string key-value pairs in the browser. Access with window.localStorage or window.sessionStorage. Both offer setItem() getItem() removeItem() and clear(). Storage events fire when values change in other tabs.

question: What is lazy loading?
answer: Lazy loading defers loading of non-critical resources until they are needed. Images can use the native attribute: . JavaScript modules can be lazily imported: import('./module.js'). This improves initial page load time.

question: What is code splitting?
answer: Code splitting breaks a JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand. Instead of one huge file, users download only the code needed for the current page. Tools like Webpack and Vite do this automatically. Dynamic import() enables manual splitting.

question: What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)?
answer: XSS attacks inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. Prevent it by never inserting untrusted data directly into HTML — use textContent instead of innerHTML. Sanitize user input on both client and server, and set a Content-Security-Policy header.

question: What is CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)?
answer: CSRF tricks authenticated users into making unintended requests. Prevent it using CSRF tokens (unique values embedded in forms and verified server-side) and the SameSite cookie attribute. Modern browsers block cross-origin cookies by default which helps.

question: What is Content Security Policy (CSP)?
answer: CSP is an HTTP response header that restricts where resources can be loaded from: Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'. It prevents XSS by blocking inline scripts and restricting external sources. Configure it on the server to only allow trusted origins.

question: What is HTTPS and why does it matter?
answer: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server using TLS. It prevents man-in-the-middle attacks, ensures data integrity, and is required for features like Service Workers and geolocation. Browsers show a padlock for HTTPS sites and warn users about HTTP sites.

question: What is tree shaking?
answer: Tree shaking is a dead code elimination technique used by bundlers like Webpack and Rollup. It analyzes ES module imports and removes unused code from the final bundle. Always use named imports instead of importing entire libraries to enable effective tree shaking.

question: What is debouncing vs throttling?
answer: Debouncing delays function execution until after a pause: good for search input (wait until user stops typing). Throttling limits how often a function runs: good for scroll events (fire at most once every 200ms). Both prevent performance issues from high-frequency events.

question: What is npm?
answer: npm (Node Package Manager) is the default package manager for Node.js. It manages project dependencies listed in package.json. Use npm install to add packages, npm run to execute scripts, and npm init to start a new project. Packages are stored in node_modules.

question: What is a bundler in web development?
answer: A bundler combines multiple JavaScript files and their dependencies into one or more optimized files for the browser. Popular bundlers include Webpack, Vite, Rollup, and Parcel. They also handle transpilation, minification, and asset optimization.

question: What is Babel?
answer: Babel is a JavaScript transpiler that converts modern JavaScript (ES6+) into older versions supported by legacy browsers. Configure it with presets like @babel/preset-env. It also supports JSX (used by React) through @babel/preset-react.

question: What is TypeScript?
answer: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static type checking: function add(a: number, b: number): number. Types catch bugs at compile time before runtime. TypeScript compiles to plain JavaScript. It is widely used in large-scale projects for better tooling and maintainability.

question: What is a linter?
answer: A linter is a tool that analyzes code for errors and style issues without running it. ESLint is the most popular JavaScript linter. It catches bugs like undefined variables, enforces coding conventions, and integrates into editors for real-time feedback and auto-fix.

question: What is Prettier?
answer: Prettier is an opinionated code formatter that automatically formats code consistently. Unlike a linter it focuses only on style (spacing, quotes, line length) not logic errors. Run it as a pre-commit hook with tools like Husky to ensure consistent style across a team.

question: What is Git and why is it used in web development?
answer: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks code changes. Create branches for features, commit changes with messages, and merge back to main. Platforms like GitHub and GitLab host repositories and enable collaboration via pull requests and code reviews.

question: What is a package.json file?
answer: package.json is the configuration file for a Node.js project. It lists metadata (name, version), dependencies (packages needed to run), devDependencies (packages needed for development), and scripts (npm commands). Share it so others can run npm install to get the same packages.

question: What is a CDN?
answer: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a network of servers distributed globally that delivers static assets from the location closest to the user. It reduces latency and load on the origin server. Libraries like Bootstrap and React are often loaded from CDNs like jsDelivr or cdnjs.

question: What is the difference between a framework and a library?
answer: A library provides tools you call when needed — you control the flow (e.g., Lodash, Axios). A framework provides a structure and calls your code — it controls the flow (e.g., Angular, Next.js). React is often called a library but its ecosystem makes it feel like a framework.

question: What is React?
answer: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces using reusable components. Each component is a function that returns JSX (HTML-like syntax). React efficiently updates the DOM by using a virtual DOM to calculate the minimum changes needed.

question: What is JSX?
answer:
JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension that looks like HTML and is used in React: const el =

Hello

. Babel compiles it to React.createElement() calls. You can embed JavaScript expressions in JSX using curly braces:

{user.name}

.

question: What are React hooks?
answer: Hooks are functions that let you use state and lifecycle features in functional components. useState manages local state, useEffect handles side effects like API calls, useContext accesses context, and useRef holds mutable values without causing re-renders.

question: What is the virtual DOM?
answer: The virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the real DOM. When state changes, React builds a new virtual DOM tree, compares it to the previous one (diffing), and updates only the changed parts in the real DOM. This is more efficient than rebuilding the entire page.

question: What is state management in frontend applications?
answer: State management handles shared data across components. Local state (useState) works for single components. Context API shares state without prop drilling. Libraries like Redux, Zustand, and Jotai manage complex global state with predictable update patterns.

question: What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?
answer: Prop drilling is passing data through many nested components just to reach a deeply nested child. Avoid it using React Context (useContext), state management libraries like Redux, or component composition patterns where you pass components as props instead of raw data.

question: What is a Single Page Application (SPA)?
answer: An SPA loads one HTML page and dynamically updates content using JavaScript instead of loading new pages. Navigation feels instant because only data (not full HTML) is fetched. React, Vue, and Angular are popular SPA frameworks. The URL changes using the History API.

question: What is server-side rendering (SSR)?
answer: SSR generates HTML on the server for each request and sends it to the browser. This improves SEO (bots see real content) and initial load performance. Next.js is the most popular React SSR framework. The opposite is CSR (client-side rendering) done entirely in the browser.

question: What is Next.js?
answer: Next.js is a React framework that adds server-side rendering, static site generation, file-based routing, and API routes. Pages in the /pages directory automatically become routes. It simplifies building production-grade React applications with built-in performance optimizations.

question: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components in React?
answer: A controlled component has its form input value managed by React state: value={state} onChange={setState}. An uncontrolled component manages its own state internally — you read its value using a ref. Controlled components give more control and are the recommended approach.

question: What is the critical rendering path?
answer: The critical rendering path is the sequence of steps the browser takes to render a page: parse HTML → build DOM, parse CSS → build CSSOM, combine into render tree, layout (compute geometry), paint (draw pixels). Optimizing it means minimizing render-blocking resources and reducing total bytes to speed up first paint.

question: What is the difference between repaint and reflow?
answer: Reflow (layout) recalculates the geometry of all elements, triggered by DOM changes that affect layout (width, height, position). Repaint only redraws pixels without changing layout (color, visibility). Reflow is expensive because it cascades; repaint is cheaper. Compositing (transform, opacity) avoids both.

question: What is the virtual DOM and how does React use it?
answer: The virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM. React renders components to a virtual DOM tree, diffs it with the previous version (reconciliation), and applies only the minimal set of changes to the real DOM. This batches updates and avoids costly direct DOM manipulation.

question: What is React's reconciliation algorithm?
answer: React's reconciliation (Fiber in React 16+) compares old and new virtual DOM trees. It uses heuristics: elements of different types are rebuilt; elements of the same type update in place; keys tell React which list items correspond across renders. Keys must be stable, unique siblings to prevent incorrect DOM reuse.

question: What is the useEffect hook and when does it run?
answer: useEffect runs after render (paint). With no dependency array it runs after every render. With an empty array [] it runs once after mount. With dependencies [a,b] it runs when a or b changes. Return a cleanup function to cancel subscriptions or timers. Replaces componentDidMount, didUpdate, and willUnmount.

question: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
answer: useMemo memoizes a computed value: useMemo(()=>expensiveCalc(a,b),[a,b]) recomputes only when a or b change. useCallback memoizes a function reference: useCallback(fn,[deps]) returns the same function object across renders unless deps change. useCallback is useMemo for functions — primarily for preventing child re-renders.

question: What is React's Context API and when should you use it?
answer: Context provides a way to pass data through the component tree without prop drilling. Create a context, wrap a subtree with Provider, and consume with useContext. Use it for global state like theme, auth, locale. Avoid for frequently-changing state (all consumers re-render on context change); prefer state management libraries in that case.

question: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled inputs in React?
answer: A controlled input has its value driven by React state (value={state} onChange={e=>setState(e.target.value)}), giving React full control. An uncontrolled input manages its own DOM state; React reads it via a ref. Controlled inputs are easier to validate and compose; uncontrolled inputs are simpler for file inputs and third-party integrations.

question: What is React Suspense and lazy loading?
answer: React.lazy(() => import('./Component')) splits code at the component boundary. Suspense wraps lazy components and shows a fallback UI while loading: <Suspense fallback={<Spinner/>}>. In React 18+, Suspense also handles async data fetching (with frameworks like Next.js). This reduces initial bundle size and improves time-to-interactive.

question: What is the Flux architecture pattern?
answer: Flux is a unidirectional data flow pattern: Action → Dispatcher → Store → View → Action. Views dispatch actions; the dispatcher sends them to stores; stores update state and emit change events; views re-render. Redux is the dominant Flux implementation, replacing the dispatcher with reducers and a single store.

question: What is Redux and what problem does it solve?
answer: Redux is a predictable state container using a single immutable store, pure reducer functions, and explicit actions. It solves prop drilling and state synchronization across distant components. The three principles: single source of truth, read-only state (actions only), changes via pure functions (reducers). DevTools enable time-travel debugging.

question: What is the difference between Redux Thunk and Redux Saga?
answer: Redux Thunk lets action creators return functions (thunks) instead of plain objects for async operations. Simple and minimal boilerplate. Redux Saga uses generator functions and effect descriptors (call, put, take) to handle complex async flows like cancellation, debouncing, and concurrency. Sagas are more testable but have a steeper learning curve.

question: What is the CSS box model?
answer: Every element is a rectangular box: content, padding (space inside the border), border, and margin (space outside). box-sizing: content-box (default) means width/height apply to content only. box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border in width/height — much more intuitive for layout and widely preferred.

question: What is CSS specificity and how is it calculated?
answer: Specificity is a weight determining which CSS rule applies when multiple rules target the same element. Calculated as (inline styles, IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements). Example: #nav .item a → 0,1,1,1 = 111. Higher specificity wins regardless of source order. !important overrides all except other !important.

question: What is the CSS cascade?
answer: The cascade is the algorithm that determines which CSS declarations apply when multiple rules conflict. Priority order: origin and importance (user-agent < author < user, normal < !important), then specificity, then source order. Understanding the cascade is essential for debugging unexpected style overrides.

question: What is a CSS pseudo-element vs pseudo-class?
answer: Pseudo-classes target elements in a specific state: :hover, :focus, :nth-child(n), :not(). Pseudo-elements target specific parts of an element: ::before, ::after (generated content), ::first-line, ::placeholder. They use different syntax (: vs ::) though browsers accept both for legacy pseudo-elements.

question: What is the difference between display: flex and display: grid?
answer: Flexbox is one-dimensional: lays out items along a main axis (row or column). Grid is two-dimensional: positions items in rows and columns simultaneously. Use flexbox for components (nav bars, card groups, centering). Use grid for page layouts and complex two-dimensional arrangements. Both can be nested.

question: What is a CSS custom property (variable)?
answer: CSS variables are defined with -- prefix and accessed via var(): :root { --color-primary: #3498db; } button { background: var(--color-primary); }. They cascade and inherit, can be updated with JavaScript, support fallbacks, and enable theming without preprocessors. Unlike Sass variables, they are resolved at runtime.

question: What is the difference between position: absolute, fixed, and sticky?
answer: absolute: positioned relative to nearest non-static ancestor; removed from normal flow. fixed: positioned relative to the viewport; stays during scroll. sticky: acts as relative until a scroll threshold, then becomes fixed within its scroll container. relative and static remain in flow; static is the default.

question: What is the CSS transform property and does it trigger reflow?
answer: transform applies geometric transformations (translate, rotate, scale, skew) without triggering layout or repaint — only compositing. The browser can offload transforms to the GPU. Using transform: translateX() instead of left: to animate position is a key performance optimization.

question: What is the difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2?
answer: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over a single TCP connection (no head-of-line blocking at HTTP layer), uses binary framing instead of text, compresses headers with HPACK, and supports server push. HTTP/1.1 pipelines requests but suffers head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 significantly reduces latency for modern web apps.

question: What is HTTP/3 and QUIC?
answer: HTTP/3 uses QUIC instead of TCP. QUIC (UDP-based) eliminates TCP handshake overhead, handles packet loss per-stream (no TCP-level head-of-line blocking), and integrates TLS 1.3 into the handshake (0-RTT reconnections). Critical for mobile networks with high packet loss. Adopted by major CDNs and browsers.

question: What is the same-origin policy and CORS?
answer: The same-origin policy prevents scripts from making requests to a different origin (protocol+host+port). CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) relaxes this: the server includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers to permit specific origins. Preflight OPTIONS requests check complex cross-origin requests before the actual request is sent.

question: What is CSP (Content Security Policy)?
answer: CSP is a browser security feature that restricts which resources (scripts, styles, images) a page can load by setting the Content-Security-Policy header. It mitigates XSS by whitelisting trusted sources: script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com. Violations can be reported to a URI. Reduces the attack surface dramatically.

question: What is HTTPS and how does TLS handshake work?
answer: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt HTTP. TLS 1.3 handshake: client sends ClientHello (supported ciphers, key share); server sends ServerHello (chosen cipher, key share, certificate); both derive session keys from the shared secret (ECDHE); client sends Finished; data flows. The handshake takes 1 RTT (0-RTT for resumptions).

question: What is JWT and how does it work?
answer: JSON Web Token is a self-contained token with three Base64URL-encoded parts: header (alg, typ), payload (claims: sub, exp, iat), and signature. The server signs with a secret (HMAC) or private key (RSA/ECDSA); clients send it in Authorization: Bearer. The server verifies the signature without DB lookup, enabling stateless auth.

question: What is OAuth 2.0?
answer: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework allowing a third party to access resources on behalf of a user without sharing credentials. Flows: Authorization Code (web apps), PKCE (SPAs/mobile), Client Credentials (machine-to-machine), Implicit (deprecated). Returns an access token and optionally a refresh token. OpenID Connect adds identity on top.

question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
answer: Authentication verifies who you are (login with password/JWT/biometrics). Authorization verifies what you can do (RBAC, permissions). Authentication precedes authorization. Example: logging in is authentication; checking whether you can access /admin is authorization.

question: What is a WebSocket?
answer: WebSockets provide full-duplex, persistent communication over a single TCP connection. After an HTTP upgrade handshake, both client and server can push messages freely with low overhead (no HTTP headers per message). Used for chat, live notifications, collaborative tools, and real-time dashboards. Unlike HTTP long-polling, no repeated connections.

question: What is Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
answer: SSE allows a server to push text events to the browser over a persistent HTTP connection (Content-Type: text/event-stream). Unlike WebSockets it is one-directional (server→client) and uses HTTP, making it firewall-friendly and auto-reconnecting. Ideal for live feeds, dashboards, and notifications that don't need bidirectional messaging.

question: What is GraphQL and how does it differ from REST?
answer: GraphQL is a query language where the client specifies exactly the data it needs in a single request. Unlike REST's fixed endpoints returning fixed shapes, GraphQL has one endpoint and returns only requested fields, solving over-fetching and under-fetching. It has strong typing, introspection, and supports mutations and subscriptions.

question: What is REST and what are its constraints?
answer: REST (Representational State Transfer) has six constraints: client-server separation, statelessness (each request contains all info), cacheability, uniform interface (resource identification, manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages, HATEOAS), layered system, and optional code-on-demand. HTTP APIs following these constraints are RESTful.

question: What is GraphQL N+1 problem and how is DataLoader solve it?
answer: In GraphQL, resolving a list of objects and then resolving a field for each (like author for each post) causes N+1 queries. DataLoader batches all individual loads in a single tick into one DB query using its batch function, then caches results within the request. This reduces N+1 to 2 queries.

question: What is a service worker?
answer: A service worker is a JavaScript worker running in a background thread, intercepting network requests to enable offline caching, push notifications, and background sync. It has a lifecycle: install (cache assets), activate (clean old caches), fetch (serve from cache or network). Required for Progressive Web Apps.

question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies?
answer: localStorage persists across sessions, no expiry, accessible only by JS, same origin (~5-10MB). sessionStorage cleared on tab close. Cookies sent with every HTTP request (server-readable), can be HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite, size limit ~4KB. Use cookies for auth tokens (HttpOnly prevents XSS); localStorage for client-side preferences.

question: What is IndexedDB?
answer: IndexedDB is a low-level browser API for storing large amounts of structured data (files, blobs, JSON) client-side. It is transactional, key-value based with indexes for querying, asynchronous, and same-origin. Storage limits are much larger than localStorage. Used in PWAs for offline data persistence.

question: What is a PWA (Progressive Web App)?
answer: A PWA is a web app that uses modern APIs to deliver app-like experiences: offline support (service worker), installability (Web App Manifest), push notifications, and fast loading. It must be served over HTTPS. PWAs can be added to the home screen and feel native without an app store.

question: What is web accessibility (a11y) and WCAG?
answer: Web accessibility ensures people with disabilities can use websites. WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) organizes guidelines under POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. Levels A, AA (most sites target), AAA. Practices: semantic HTML, ARIA roles, keyboard navigation, color contrast ≥4.5:1, alt text.

question: What is ARIA and when should you use it?
answer: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) provides attributes (role, aria-label, aria-expanded, aria-live) to supplement HTML semantics for assistive technologies. First rule: use native HTML elements (button, nav, input) which have built-in semantics. Only use ARIA when no native element meets the need. Incorrect ARIA is worse than none.

question: What is lazy loading for images and how is it implemented?
answer: Lazy loading defers loading off-screen images until they approach the viewport, reducing initial page load. Native: . Intersection Observer API in JavaScript detects when an image enters the viewport and swaps data-src into src. Reduces initial payload, improves LCP and TTI metrics.

question: What is tree shaking?
answer: Tree shaking removes unused exports from JavaScript bundles by static analysis. Bundlers (webpack, Rollup) trace the import/export graph and eliminate dead code. Requires ES modules (static imports); CommonJS require() is not tree-shakable. Significantly reduces bundle size for libraries like lodash-es vs lodash.

question: What is code splitting?
answer: Code splitting divides a bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand. In webpack: dynamic import() creates split points. React.lazy() wraps components for route-level splitting. Reduces initial JS payload; only code for the current route is loaded. Combined with prefetching, it can minimize both initial and subsequent loads.

question: What is the difference between Webpack and Vite?
answer: Webpack bundles all modules ahead of time using CommonJS/ESM, good for complex configs but slow cold starts. Vite serves source files as native ESM in development (no bundling, instant HMR via browser module reloading) and uses Rollup for optimized production builds. Vite has dramatically faster dev startup for large apps.

question: What is the difference between SSR, SSG, and CSR?
answer: CSR (Client-Side Rendering) sends a minimal HTML shell; JS builds the DOM in the browser — poor SEO, slow first paint. SSR (Server-Side Rendering) renders full HTML per request on the server — good SEO, TTFB depends on server. SSG (Static Site Generation) pre-renders at build time — best performance, limited to non-personalized content.

question: What is ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration)?
answer: ISR (Next.js feature) serves statically generated pages and regenerates them in the background at a defined interval (revalidate: 60 seconds). Users get cached pages (fast) while stale pages are updated without rebuilding the whole site. Combines SSG's performance with SSR's freshness.

question: What is the difference between a cookie's HttpOnly and SameSite attributes?
answer: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie (mitigates XSS theft). SameSite controls cross-site sending: Strict (never sent cross-site), Lax (sent on top-level navigation GET, default in modern browsers), None (sent always, requires Secure). SameSite=Lax/Strict mitigates CSRF attacks without needing a CSRF token.

question: What is XSS and how do you prevent it?
answer: Cross-Site Scripting injects malicious scripts into pages viewed by other users. Types: stored (persisted in DB), reflected (in response to crafted request), DOM-based (client-side only). Prevention: escape HTML output (textContent not innerHTML), CSP headers, HttpOnly cookies, sanitize user input, avoid eval().

question: What is CSRF and how do you prevent it?
answer: Cross-Site Request Forgery tricks a user's browser into making an authenticated request to your site from another origin. Prevention: SameSite cookies (Lax/Strict), CSRF tokens (random token in form/header verified server-side), checking Origin/Referer headers. SameSite=Lax blocks most CSRF without tokens.

question: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it in a web app?
answer: SQL injection inserts malicious SQL into query parameters. Example: ' OR 1=1 -- bypasses login. Prevention: parameterized queries / prepared statements (never string-concatenate user input into SQL), ORMs, input validation. Principle of least privilege: DB user should only have needed permissions.

question: What is the event loop in JavaScript?
answer: JavaScript is single-threaded with an event loop. The call stack runs synchronous code. When async work completes, callbacks are queued: microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) have priority over macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O). After each task, all microtasks run before the next macrotask. This defines async execution order.

question: What is the difference between Promise and async/await?
answer: async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises. async functions return Promises; await pauses execution within the function until a Promise resolves. Error handling uses try/catch instead of .catch(). Both are non-blocking. async/await makes asynchronous code read synchronously and is easier to debug with stack traces.

question: What is Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled?
answer: Promise.all takes an array of promises and resolves with an array of results when all resolve; rejects immediately if any rejects (fail-fast). Promise.allSettled waits for all to settle and returns an array of {status, value/reason} objects regardless of failures. Use allSettled when you need results from all even if some fail.

question: What is the JavaScript prototype chain?
answer: Every JS object has a hidden [[Prototype]] link. Property lookup walks the chain: if a property isn't on the object, JS looks at its prototype, then that prototype's prototype, up to Object.prototype (null). Constructors set obj.__proto__ = Constructor.prototype. class syntax is syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance.

question: What is closure in JavaScript?
answer: A closure is a function that remembers its lexical scope even when executed outside it. The inner function captures variables from the outer function's environment. Used for data encapsulation, factory functions, and callbacks. Common in module patterns and event handlers. Memory consideration: closures keep outer scope alive as long as they exist.

question: What is the difference between var, let, and const?
answer: var is function-scoped, hoisted to the top of its function, can be re-declared. let and const are block-scoped, hoisted but not initialized (temporal dead zone). const requires initialization and cannot be reassigned (but the object it references can be mutated). Always prefer const; use let when reassignment is needed; avoid var.

question: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
answer: Hoisting moves declarations (not initializations) to the top of their scope during compilation. var declarations are hoisted and initialized to undefined. Function declarations are fully hoisted. let/const are hoisted but not initialized — accessing them before declaration throws a ReferenceError (Temporal Dead Zone).

question: What is debouncing vs throttling?
answer: Debouncing delays a function call until after a pause in events (e.g., wait 300ms after last keystroke before searching). Throttling ensures a function runs at most once per interval regardless of event frequency (e.g., scroll handler at most every 100ms). Debounce for 'when done typing'; throttle for 'rate limit'.

question: What is the Intersection Observer API?
answer: Intersection Observer asynchronously notifies when a target element intersects a root element or the viewport. Avoids expensive scroll event listeners and getBoundingClientRect() calls. Used for lazy loading, infinite scroll, and analytics (tracking when elements enter view). Callbacks run off the main thread in batches.

question: What is WebAssembly (WASM)?
answer: WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that runs in browsers at near-native speed. Languages like C, C++, and Rust compile to WASM. It runs in the same sandbox as JavaScript, shares the JS event loop, and has a structured API. Used for compute-heavy tasks: video editing, games, CAD, and scientific simulations in browsers.

question: What is the difference between a framework and a library?
answer: A library provides utilities you call (React, Lodash — you control the flow). A framework provides a structure your code plugs into (Angular, Next.js — the framework calls your code, inversion of control). Frameworks are opinionated and reduce decisions; libraries are flexible but require more architectural decisions.

question: What is micro-frontend architecture?
answer: Micro-frontends apply microservice principles to the frontend: independent teams build, deploy, and own separate UI features. Integration methods: iframes (isolation but poor UX), web components, module federation (webpack shares runtime modules), or server-side composition. Enables independent deployments but adds complexity in routing and shared state.

question: What is Module Federation in Webpack?
answer: Module Federation allows separately built and deployed webpack bundles to share modules at runtime. A host app loads remote apps' components as if they were local. Enables true micro-frontend architecture where teams deploy independently without a monolithic build. Versioning and shared dependencies (like React) must be carefully configured.

question: What is a CDN and how does it improve performance?
answer: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) distributes static assets across geographically distributed edge servers. Users receive assets from the nearest edge node, reducing latency. CDNs also cache dynamic content, handle DDoS mitigation, provide TLS termination, and reduce origin server load. Critical for global web performance.

question: What is the difference between long polling and WebSockets?
answer: Long polling: client sends request; server holds it open until data is available, then responds; client immediately sends another request. Simulates push with standard HTTP but has overhead per cycle. WebSockets maintain a persistent connection with full-duplex messaging — much lower overhead for frequent messages. SSE is a simpler alternative for server→client only.

question: What is the purpose of the meta viewport tag?
answer: <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'> tells the browser to set the viewport width to the device width and not zoom out. Without it, mobile browsers render at a virtual 980px and zoom out, breaking responsive designs. Required for responsive layouts using CSS media queries.

question: What is a CSS media query?
answer: Media queries apply CSS rules based on device characteristics: @media (max-width: 768px) { ... } or @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { ... }. Used for responsive design (mobile-first: base styles for small screens, add complexity at larger breakpoints). Also targets print, screen resolution, and user accessibility preferences.

question: What is the difference between mobile-first and desktop-first CSS?
answer: Mobile-first writes base styles for small screens and uses min-width media queries to add complexity for larger screens. Desktop-first writes for large screens and uses max-width queries to simplify for smaller ones. Mobile-first is preferred because most traffic is mobile; performance is better as mobile users don't download desktop-only CSS.

question: What is the web vitals metric LCP, FID, and CLS?
answer: Core Web Vitals: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measures loading performance — target <2.5s. FID (First Input Delay, replaced by INP — Interaction to Next Paint) measures interactivity — INP target <200ms. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures visual stability — target <0.1. These are Google ranking signals.

question: What is lazy evaluation vs eager evaluation in JavaScript?
answer: Eager evaluation computes values immediately when assigned or passed. Lazy evaluation defers computation until the value is needed. In JS: || and && short-circuit (lazy); generators yield values on demand; optional chaining ?. skips evaluation if null/undefined. Lazy patterns improve performance by avoiding unnecessary work.

question: What is a web component?
answer: Web components are a set of browser APIs for creating reusable custom HTML elements: Custom Elements (define new tags), Shadow DOM (encapsulated DOM/styles), and HTML templates (<template>/<slot>). Framework-agnostic and natively supported. Used for cross-framework design systems. Shadow DOM's style encapsulation prevents CSS leakage.

question: What is the Shadow DOM?
answer: Shadow DOM attaches a private, encapsulated DOM tree to an element. Styles inside it don't leak out and external styles don't bleed in (unless CSS custom properties are used). Used in web components and browser built-ins like <video> controls. Enables true component-level style isolation without CSS-in-JS or BEM conventions.

question: What is TypeScript and what advantages does it offer?
answer: TypeScript is a statically typed superset of JavaScript compiled to plain JS. It catches type errors at compile time, improves IDE autocompletion and refactoring, and serves as documentation. Generics, interfaces, and unions make complex data shapes explicit. Gradual adoption: .js can be .ts incrementally. Used by React, Angular, Vue 3.

question: What is the difference between interface and type in TypeScript?
answer: interface defines object shapes and can be extended or implemented by classes; declaration merging allows adding to existing interfaces. type is an alias for any type including primitives, unions, and tuples; cannot be re-opened. In practice both are often interchangeable for object shapes; use interface for public APIs, type for complex unions.

question: What are TypeScript generics?
answer: Generics allow writing reusable code that works with multiple types while retaining type safety: function identity<T>(arg: T): T { return arg; }. Used in collections, utilities, and API wrappers. Constraints: <T extends Serializable> limits T. Generic interfaces and classes enable type-safe data structures like Stack<T>.

question: What is tree shaking and how does it relate to ES modules?
answer: Tree shaking relies on ES module syntax (import/export) because imports are static and analyzable at build time. Bundlers trace the dependency graph and drop unexported code. CommonJS require() is dynamic — the module may export different things at runtime — so it cannot be tree-shaken. Always use named ESM imports for tree-shakable libraries.

question: What is a headless CMS?
answer: A headless CMS manages content but has no frontend presentation layer — content is delivered via API (REST or GraphQL) to any frontend (web, mobile, IoT). Examples: Contentful, Strapi, Sanity. Decouples content from presentation, enabling omnichannel delivery. Contrasts with coupled CMSes like WordPress where templates are built-in.

question: What is edge computing in the context of web development?
answer: Edge computing runs server-side code at geographically distributed edge nodes (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge Functions) close to users instead of a centralized data center. Reduces latency for personalized content, A/B testing, authentication, and geo-routing. Works on limited runtimes (no Node.js-specific APIs); ideal for lightweight request handling.

question: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic UI updates?
answer: Optimistic update immediately reflects the expected server response in the UI before the request completes — if it fails, the UI reverts. Pessimistic update waits for server confirmation before updating the UI, showing a loading state. Optimistic is faster-feeling for reliable operations (likes, todo toggle); pessimistic for critical data (payments).

question: What is a design token?
answer: Design tokens are named, platform-agnostic variables for design decisions: colors, spacing, typography, shadows. Defined once (e.g., --color-brand-primary: #3498db) and consumed across web, iOS, Android, and print. Tools like Theo or Style Dictionary transform tokens to platform-specific formats, ensuring visual consistency across products.

question: What is the difference between monorepo and polyrepo?
answer: A monorepo stores multiple packages/apps in one repository. Enables atomic commits, shared tooling, easy refactoring across packages, and consistent CI. Tools: Turborepo, Nx, Lerna. A polyrepo keeps each package separately — clearer ownership and independent deployment. Monorepos become complex at scale; polyrepos have duplication and version synchronization overhead.

question: What is semantic versioning (SemVer)?
answer: SemVer uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backwards-compatible features, PATCH for backwards-compatible bug fixes. Allows consumers to safely update using ranges (^1.2.3 allows up to <2.0.0; ~1.2.3 allows up to <1.3.0). Enables lock files in npm/yarn to guarantee reproducible builds.

question: What is a linter and how does ESLint work?
answer: A linter statically analyzes code for style and quality issues. ESLint parses JS/TS into an AST and applies configurable rules (no-unused-vars, react-hooks/rules-of-hooks). Rules can warn or error; some are auto-fixable. Integrates with CI and editors. Prettier handles formatting (non-opinionated on style); ESLint handles code quality rules.

question: What is the purpose of a .env file and how should secrets be handled?
answer: .env files store environment-specific configuration (API keys, DB URLs) outside source code. They are loaded into process.env by libraries like dotenv. Never commit .env to version control; use .env.example as a template. For production, use proper secret management (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, platform env vars) rather than .env files.

question: What is Docker and how does it benefit web development?
answer: Docker packages an app with its dependencies into a container — a reproducible environment that runs identically on any host. Eliminates 'works on my machine'. Key concepts: Dockerfile (build instructions), image (built artifact), container (running instance). Docker Compose orchestrates multi-service development (app + DB + cache). Used for consistent dev, test, and prod environments.

question: What is CI/CD?
answer: CI (Continuous Integration) automatically builds and tests code on every push, catching integration bugs early. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) automatically deploys code to staging or production after CI passes. A pipeline: push → lint → test → build → deploy. Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI. Enables rapid, reliable releases.

question: What is OWASP and what are the Top 10 web security risks?
answer: OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project) maintains the Top 10 most critical web risks. Current top items include: Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection (SQL/XSS), Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration, Vulnerable and Outdated Components, Authentication Failures, Software Integrity Failures, Logging Failures, and SSRF. A checklist for secure development.

question: What is rate limiting and why is it important?
answer: Rate limiting restricts how many requests a client can make in a time window. Prevents brute-force attacks (login), API abuse, DDoS amplification, and cost overruns. Implemented with a token bucket or leaky bucket algorithm. Response: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header. Applies per IP, user, or API key.

question: What is a reverse proxy and how does Nginx fit into a web stack?
answer: A reverse proxy accepts client requests and forwards them to backend servers, hiding server topology. Nginx acts as a reverse proxy: SSL termination, load balancing, static file serving, gzip compression, and caching. Sitting in front of Node.js/Python apps it handles high concurrency efficiently (event-driven, non-blocking I/O) while apps focus on business logic.

question: What is horizontal vs vertical scaling?
answer: Vertical scaling (scale up) adds more CPU/RAM to a single server — simple but has hardware limits and single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more server instances behind a load balancer — no theoretical limit, high availability, but requires stateless apps (sessions in Redis, not local memory) and distributed data management.

question: What is a load balancer and what algorithms does it use?
answer: A load balancer distributes traffic across server instances. Algorithms: Round Robin (equal turn), Least Connections (to least busy server), IP Hash (consistent routing by client IP for session affinity), Weighted Round Robin (proportional to capacity). Layer 4 (TCP) is fast; Layer 7 (HTTP) enables content-based routing. Examples: Nginx, AWS ALB, HAProxy.

question: What is caching at different levels in a web stack?
answer: Browser cache (HTTP headers: Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified). CDN cache (edge, reduced origin load). Reverse proxy cache (Nginx, Varnish). Application cache (in-memory: Redis, Memcached — query results, session). DB query cache (deprecated in MySQL 8; use ORM-level caching). Database buffer pool (disk page cache). Each level trades freshness for speed.

question: What is the difference between Redis and Memcached?
answer: Redis is an advanced key-value store supporting rich data types (list, hash, set, sorted set, stream), persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF log), pub/sub, Lua scripting, and clustering. Memcached is simpler: pure key-value, in-memory only, multi-threaded. Use Redis for most cases; Memcached for extreme simplicity or multi-threaded throughput.

question: What is a message queue and when would you use one?
answer: A message queue (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) decouples producers from consumers for async processing. Use cases: email sending (fire and forget), order processing, background jobs, event streaming. Benefits: absorbs traffic spikes, enables retry on failure, decouples services. Kafka is durable and replay-capable; RabbitMQ is a traditional broker for task queues.

question: What is database sharding?
answer: Sharding horizontally partitions a database by splitting data across multiple DB instances by a shard key (e.g., user ID range or hash). Each shard handles a subset of data, reducing per-node load and enabling horizontal scaling. Challenges: cross-shard queries, rebalancing when adding shards, and hotspots if the key is poorly chosen.

question: What is an ORM and what are its trade-offs?
answer: An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) maps database tables to language objects (Sequelize, TypeORM, Prisma for JS; SQLAlchemy for Python). Benefits: type safety, less boilerplate SQL, DB portability. Trade-offs: N+1 queries if relations aren't eagerly loaded, abstraction leakage for complex queries, performance overhead vs hand-tuned SQL. Always check generated queries in production.

question: What is the CAP theorem?
answer: CAP states a distributed system can guarantee at most two of three: Consistency (all nodes see the same data), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition Tolerance (operates despite network partitions). Since partitions are unavoidable in distributed networks, systems choose CP (strong consistency — HBase, ZooKeeper) or AP (available, eventually consistent — Cassandra, DynamoDB).

question: What is eventual consistency?
answer: Eventual consistency means all replicas will converge to the same value given no new writes, but at any point replicas may differ. Used in distributed databases (DynamoDB, Cassandra) for high availability. Suitable for non-critical data (shopping cart, view counts). Contrast with strong consistency (reads always see latest write) which requires coordination overhead.

question: What is gRPC and when would you use it over REST?
answer: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers (binary serialization) over HTTP/2 for high-performance, strongly typed RPC. Supports bidirectional streaming, code generation for clients/servers in many languages, and smaller payloads than JSON. Use for internal microservice communication where performance matters; REST/GraphQL for public-facing APIs where tooling and readability matter.

question: What is a monolith vs microservices architecture?
answer: A monolith is a single deployable unit — all features in one codebase. Simple to develop initially, easy to test, but hard to scale individual features and becomes complex at scale. Microservices split functionality into independently deployable services communicating via APIs/message queues. Enables independent scaling and deployment but adds network complexity, distributed tracing needs, and operational overhead.

question: What is OpenAPI / Swagger?
answer: OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is a specification for describing REST APIs in YAML/JSON. It documents endpoints, request/response schemas, authentication, and parameters. Tools generate interactive docs (Swagger UI), client SDKs, and server stubs from the spec. Contract-first API design (write the spec before code) aligns frontend and backend teams early.
